To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in regular marijuana smokers, the immediate effects (i.e., the acute pharmacologic effects) of marijuana may impact cognitive–motor skills, and brain mechanisms that are related to coordinated movement.

17 mg of THC increased brain activity during a virtual reality driving task in the frontal and anterior cingulated cortices and reduced brain activity in the occipitals, and increased wall hits in the virtual reality driving maze task.

17 mg of Δ9-THC, the main psychoactive constituent of marijuana, increases brain metabolism during a virtual reality maze performance task in areas associated with attention and motor coordination, and decreases metabolism in areas related to visual integration in regular users of cannabis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the acute effects of marijuana use on brain function and behavior in regular users of the drug.
the effects of marijuana on brain function, and in particular with the effects of acute marijuana use on brain function in individuals with a history of regular marijuana use.
the effects of cannabis and cannabis use on the brain and behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

17 mg Δ9-tetrahidrocannabinol (TH) in a single dose in regular marijuana users may impact on cognitive-motor skills and brain mechanisms involved in the modulation of coordinated movement and driving.

17 mg Δ9-tetrahdyrocannabinol (THCMg) increased metabolism in the middle and anterior cingulated cortices and anterior frontal lobes during a virtual maze task, and decreased metabolism in the posterior occipital lob.
marijuana use can impair cognitive–motor skills.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the acute administration of THC impairs the performance of a complex cognitive task in marijuana users, and this is associated with changes in brain function in regions that are involved in attention and motor coordination.
THC impairs the ability to control movement and attention, and that the acute effects of THC on the brain may contribute to the risk of accidents in regular marijuana users.
the acute effects of marijuana on attention and motor skills may be mediated by changes in brain metabolism in the frontal and occipital regions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
marijuana can have acute effects on the brain, and that these effects are different in heavy marijuana users compared to non-users.
THC can impair driving skills and attention.
marijuana use is associated with increased risk for traffic crashes and that marijuana users are more likely to crash while high than while abstinent.
